You can run NameQuick in automatic mode and let it rename files as they arrive, or in review mode where you can manually check renames before they’re approved. And it won’t guess – if it’s not certain it can rename a file it’ll wait for you to fill in the missing details so that you know it’s correct. NameQuick only works on the files and folders you select and nothing else changes – the file date and folders remain untouched. articles.excerpt: Accueil > LOGISTIQUE , LEGISLATION , MARKETPLACE > TVA e-commerce : l’UE veut étendre l’IOSS aux commandes de plus de 150 € L’Union européenne prépare une nouvelle évolution de la fiscalité du e-commerce transfrontalier. Le 9 novembre 2026, les ministres européens des Finances se sont accordés sur un projet visant à étendre l’Import One-Stop Shop (IOSS) aux commandes d’une valeur supérieure à 150 euros . Aujourd’hui, ce guichet unique permettant de collecter et déclarer la TVA sur certaines importations est limité aux envois ne dépassant pas ce seuil. Pour les marketplaces et vendeurs cross-border, la réforme déplacerait davantage la gestion de la TVA vers le checkout : celle-ci pourrait être collectée dès la commande puis déclarée via un seul État membre, y compris pour des achats dépassant 150 euros. Le Parlement européen doit encore être consulté avant l’adoption formelle du texte, avec une entrée en vigueur envisagée au 1er juillet 2028 . L’IOSS permet aux vendeurs établis hors de l’Union européenne, ou aux plateformes qui facilitent leurs ventes, de collecter la TVA au moment du paiement puis de la déclarer via un seul État membre, même lorsque leurs clients se trouvent dans plusieurs pays européens. Aujourd’hui, ce mécanisme s’arrête à 150 euros par envoi . Le projet européen supprimerait cette limite pour les marchandises éligibles. Les produits soumis à accises resteraient en dehors du dispositif. Une précision est essentielle : il ne s’agit pas de créer une nouvelle TVA sur les commandes supérieures à 150 euros . Les importations commerciales sont déjà soumises à la TVA quelle que soit leur valeur. La réforme modifie surtout le moment de sa collecte et le circuit utilisé pour la déclarer . articles.excerpt: Google Ads’ all-or-nothing channel targeting has long frustrated advertisers. Campaign types offer little flexibility for choosing ad channels. For example, Performance Max campaigns show across all of Google Search, Discover, Gmail, Maps, YouTube, and the Display Network. Similarly, Search campaigns show on Google’s Search partners, or not. There is no in-between. Last month Google announced a feature called “channel prioritization” to set “High” or “Low” priorities for each channel. Toggle a channel to Low priority, and Google Ads will show its 28-day spend percentage. In the screenshot below, 26.3% of Performance Max spend had gone to the Display Network. Yet by itself the percentage doesn’t tell us whether to prioritize. With “channel prioritization,” advertisers can assign a “High” or “Low” priority for each channel. The channel performance report, in the “Insights and reports” section, provides the bottom-line conversion data. In this example, the overall campaign had 77 conversions and, as shown below, 37 came from the Display Network. That’s 48.1% of conversions (37 ÷ 77) for 26.3% of the spend. The channel performance report provides the bottom-line conversion data. We can thus conclude the channel is performing comparatively well. It’s a “High priority.” Other channels, however, could have a relatively large spend for the conversion count. They are a “Low priority,” and advertisers can enter a max daily-spend percentage. Advertisers can set channel prioritization at the account or campaign level for each campaign type. For example, an advertiser could set Performance Max campaigns to Low priority for all “Google channels.” Accounts with few campaigns will likely opt for account-level settings, while accounts with many campaigns should prioritize for each one.

articles.excerpt: As our models get more powerful and the associated safety and security risks become bigger, it becomes more and more critical that we can detect potential issues, and quickly stop models in their tracks when needed. It connects every research inference workload, including agentic sampling for model training and evaluation, data processing, and more. This works together with our misalignment monitoring systems , and halts model output within 35 seconds of a decision to intervene to stop or pause a job. articles.summary: The question is not what AI agents can do. It is what they are allowed to do and who remains accountable. The post Who Owns an AI Agent’s Mistakes? appeared first on Practical Ecommerce .
articles.excerpt: Merchants who let AI agents act autonomously should first assign responsibility for mistakes or extreme risks. “Once an agent can update a product catalog, issue a refund, or change a campaign, it becomes operational software with delegated business authority. The company needs to treat it that way,” wrote David Greenberg, chief marketing officer at BlueRock Security , a cybersecurity company. Businesses, including ecommerce shops, are evolving from experimenting with AI to deploying agents in production or customer-facing applications. Consider an ecommerce merchant that instructs an AI agent to improve conversion rates for underperforming products. The agent might examine inventory, identify slow-selling items, reduce prices, and shift advertising spending toward those products. Each action could be reasonable, but the combined result might undermine margins, exhaust inventory, or create unexpected costs. The question then is how much authority the merchant should delegate. The Massachusetts Institute of Technology’s Center for Information Systems Research identified two factors — ambiguity and risk — to determine which decisions AI should make. Routine tasks with predictable outcomes and limited consequences are good candidates for automation. But matters involving uncertainty, significant financial exposure, or competing objectives warrant greater human involvement. articles.excerpt: In every aspect of Oner Active’s new flagship store, opening in Manhattan this week, brand founder Krissy Cela wanted to set Oner apart from other activewear brands. For one, the custom scent she created for the store has notes of tequila in it. “We refuse to be a brand that’s based on green juice and matcha,” she said. “I want more tequila than wheatgrass. Scents have associations, like cinnamon and Christmas. So when you come into the store and you smell tequila, you’re not going to be thinking about anything but a good time.” It’s one of the many thoughtful touches Cela and the team have put into the new 5,000-square-foot flagship store on Bond Street downtown. Others include a “boyfriend couch” in the middle of the store and large mirrors with the Oner logo printed on them. The mirror logo is offset to the side so customers have enough room to take some mirror selfies for social media while still capturing the brand name in the image. “We’re such a social-first business, so that was quite important to us,” Cela said. “I know our girls are going to take selfies.” Cela started as a fitness trainer, then fitness influencer, before founding Oner in 2020. Oner is now projecting to reach over $250 million in revenue this year with zero outside funding.
